warmup.q: Two regions each run a leader that takes writes for the same payments table, and they copy each other's changes, usually within a second. A payment times out, and the card reader tries again in the other region 200 ms later. Both tries carry the same payment key, a unique label the app gives each payment. Each region charges the card only if it can store that key, and it refuses a key it already has. How many charges?
options: One: the second region refuses the key it already has
Two, if the retry arrives before the first key has been copied over: each region checks only its own copy
One: the copying always delivers the first key before the second region saves anything
None: the two writes clash and both are undone
warmup.why: Each leader looks for the key in its own copy of the table. With copies up to a second behind, the second region hasn't seen the first key 200 ms later, so it stores the key too, and both regions charge the card. The check is real, but it runs against an incomplete copy. When the two rows later meet, a rule (often: keep the later one) keeps one of them, but the card was already charged twice. Nothing is undone, because each region had already said OK.

sections.h: A leader in each region: fast local writes, and two regions that write the same row
sections.html:
Let's put exact numbers on the opening. In One leader, many followers (lesson 1), a leader was the one server that takes every write and puts it in order in its log. It sends that log to its followers, which copy it. Keeping copies like this on several machines is replication.

A card reader in Frankfurt places a hold for the shop M-0042. A hold asks for an amount to be set aside on the card until the payment goes through, the way a hotel does when you check in. If the only leader is in Virginia, the write crosses the Atlantic and comes back before the reader hears OK. One round trip takes about 70 ms. A transaction, a group of changes saved together, made of four statements that each wait for an answer, takes 280 ms. And when the link across the ocean fails, or the Virginia data center (a building full of servers) does, Frankfurt can't write at all. It waits until someone fails over to a copy elsewhere, with the risks lesson 1 described.

The simplest fix is a leader in each region, a group of data centers in one part of the world. The code calls the Frankfurt leader eu and the Virginia leader us. eu saves its own customers' writes and answers in about a millisecond, and us does the same for its customers. Each leader also sends its log to the other, as rows inserted, updated and deleted (the logical log of Replication logs, lesson 2). And it applies the other's log the way a follower would. So each region is a leader for its own customers and a follower of every other leader. That's multi-leader replication.

Picture two cafés that each keep a copy of the same notebook. Each café writes new lines in its own copy at once, and phones the other café its new lines a moment later. The notebooks are the databases, each café is a leader, and the phone calls carry the logs.

The phone call has to come after the answer, which makes the copying asynchronous. If eu waited for us before answering, every write would pay the 70 ms again, and a broken link would stop writes in both regions. That's one leader with extra parts.

Three kinds of system end up with this shape. Several regions, as here. Devices that keep working offline: a laptop on a train is a region whose copy is two hours behind, which is the next lesson. And shared editing, where each person's typing appears in their own copy before any server has seen it.

The new problem fits in two writes. At 10:00:00.000, eu adds hold h-eu to M-0042's list of open holds, one row in a table, and confirms it. Ten milliseconds later, before that change has crossed the ocean, us adds h-us to its own copy and confirms that. Both customers were told OK. Now each region holds a version of the row that the other has never seen. That's a write conflict: both cafés changed the same page before either phoned. When the changes arrive, each leader must do something with a row that doesn't match what it expected.

Conflicts aren't the only cost. Any rule that has to see every write stops working: a payment key that must be unique, a balance that must stay at zero or above. Each leader checks the rule against its own copy, and both copies can pass. Inside one data center, a round trip takes about half a millisecond, so a second leader buys almost nothing for these costs. Multi-leader is a tool for regions and for offline devices.

A conflict is one row with a write in each leader's log that the other leader hasn't seen. The rest of the lesson asks how the logs travel, and what to do when they disagree.

try.title: Two confirmed writes, one survivor
steps: Read FirstConflictDemo.kt. It prints a timeline with one leader in us, then with a leader in each region, 35 ms apart one way. It settles the conflict with last write wins: every change carries a timestamp, the time on its leader's clock, and every leader keeps the change with the later one.
Predict which hold survives, then run it from the labs folder. No Docker needed.
Change the us write's timestamp from 10 to -5, as if the us clock ran 15 ms behind, and run it again. Predict the survivor first.
try.expect:
-- one leader, in us --
t=0    eu  client sends: add hold h-eu
t=35   us  leader commits [h-eu]
t=70   eu  client gets OK after 70 ms; a 4-statement transaction would wait 280 ms

-- a leader in each region --
t=0    eu  leader commits [h-eu] at ts 0, client gets OK after 1 ms
t=10   us  leader commits [h-us] at ts 10, client gets OK after 1 ms
t=35   us  receives [h-eu] from eu; its own [h-us] never saw it: a conflict
t=45   eu  receives [h-us] from us; its own [h-eu] never saw it: a conflict

last write wins keeps ts 10 from us:  eu = [h-us]   us = [h-us]
acknowledged: h-eu, h-us   kept: [h-us]   lost: [h-eu]

Both customers heard OK after 1 ms, and both regions end with the same value, so the copying "worked". One acknowledged hold, a hold its customer was told was saved, is gone, and no one was told. With the us timestamp at -5, the last two lines become keeps ts 0 from eu and lost: [h-us]. The write made second now loses, because a clock decided, not the order of events.

sections.h: Circles, stars and all-to-all: how the logs travel, and the update that overtakes its insert
sections.html:
With two leaders, each sends its log to the other. With three or more, someone has to decide who sends to whom. The shape of those links is the topology, and three are common. In a circle, each leader forwards to the next one: eu to us, us to ap (Asia and the Pacific), and ap back to eu. A change reaches the far side by hopping through the others. In a star, one hub receives every leader's changes and forwards them to the rest. In all-to-all, every leader sends its changes straight to every other.

Forwarding makes a loop at once. If us forwards everything it applies, eu's change comes back to eu, which forwards it again, forever. So every change carries the name of the leader where it was first written, its origin. In a circle or a star, it also carries the names of the nodes (servers) it has passed through, and a node drops a change it has already applied. PostgreSQL, a free database program, can copy row changes between servers with its logical replication, and it records the origin of each change it applies. A subscription, the setting on one server that pulls changes from another, created with origin = none asks for local changes only. So two servers can subscribe to each other without echoing.

Circles and stars each depend on single nodes. A dead hub stops all copying, and a dead node in a circle cuts the chain until someone rewires it. All-to-all has no such node, which is why it's the usual choice. Its weakness is quieter: changes take different links at different speeds, so a later change can overtake an earlier one.

The stepper shows a real case, with two words for a card payment's steps. When you tap, your bank sets the money aside and the payment is AUTHORIZED. Later the money really moves, and it's CAPTURED. eu inserts payment pay-81723 as AUTHORIZED. us gets the insert after 40 ms and captures the payment at 45 ms, an UPDATE to CAPTURED. Today ap's link from eu is slow, 150 ms, while us reaches ap in 30 ms. So ap gets the UPDATE at 75 ms, for a row it doesn't have yet.

pgactive, a free add-on from Amazon that lets several PostgreSQL servers all take writes, documents its default for exactly this case: discard the UPDATE. Its documentation warns that this "can result in data inconsistencies across nodes". When the insert lands at 150 ms, ap says AUTHORIZED, the others say CAPTURED, and nothing will ever repair it.

You may be thinking that timestamps fix it: every leader keeps whichever version carries the later time. But if us's clock runs 60 ms behind eu's, the capture is stamped before the insert, and every region throws the capture away. The regions agree, on the wrong answer.

What works is to carry causality, what each change had already seen, instead of time. The update records what us had applied when it made the change: eu's change number 1. ap holds the update until it has applied that change too, then applies both in order. That record, one counter per leader, is a version vector, and Concurrent writes (lesson 8) builds it properly.

Holding the update fixes the order, because the update had seen the insert. Next, we'll face the harder case: two writes that really didn't see each other.

stepper.title: An update overtakes its insert in all-to-all replication

try.title: Three ways to treat an update that arrives early
steps: Read the delays at the top of OvertakeDemo.kt. Then predict the final line of each of its three runs: discard, timestamps with the us clock 60 ms behind, and causal.
In main, change run("timestamps", -60) to run("timestamps", 60) and run it again. Timestamps now give the right answer. Ask yourself what made the difference.
try.expect:
-- discard --
  t=0   eu applies INSERT AUTHORIZED
  t=40  us applies INSERT AUTHORIZED
  t=45  us applies UPDATE CAPTURED
  t=75  ap discards UPDATE CAPTURED: no such row
  t=85  eu applies UPDATE CAPTURED
  t=150 ap applies INSERT AUTHORIZED
  final: eu=CAPTURED  us=CAPTURED  ap=AUTHORIZED

-- timestamps, us clock -60 ms off --
  t=0   eu applies INSERT AUTHORIZED
  t=40  us applies INSERT AUTHORIZED
  t=45  us ignores UPDATE CAPTURED: ts -15 < 0
  t=75  ap applies UPDATE CAPTURED
  t=85  eu ignores UPDATE CAPTURED: ts -15 < 0
  t=150 ap applies INSERT AUTHORIZED
  final: eu=AUTHORIZED  us=AUTHORIZED  ap=AUTHORIZED

-- causal --
  t=0   eu applies INSERT AUTHORIZED
  t=40  us applies INSERT AUTHORIZED
  t=45  us applies UPDATE CAPTURED
  t=75  ap holds UPDATE CAPTURED: it needs {eu=1} first
  t=85  eu applies UPDATE CAPTURED
  t=150 ap applies INSERT AUTHORIZED
  t=150 ap applies UPDATE CAPTURED
  final: eu=CAPTURED  us=CAPTURED  ap=CAPTURED

Discarding leaves the regions apart for good. Timestamps make them agree, but on the version without the capture, and even us ignores its own capture because its stamp is older. With the clock 60 ms ahead instead, the timestamps run ends eu=CAPTURED us=CAPTURED ap=CAPTURED (ap ignores the late insert: ts 0 < 105). Same events, opposite outcome: timestamps are right only when the clocks happen to agree with the order of events. The causal run is right whatever the clocks say.

sections.h: Handling a conflict: avoid it, let the last write win, or keep both
sections.html:
Two writes conflict when neither leader had seen the other's write when it accepted its own. The clock doesn't decide it. Two laptops that change a shop's details offline, an hour apart, conflict. Two writes 2 ms apart don't, if the second one's leader had already applied the first. Such writes are called concurrent, and Concurrent writes (lesson 8) makes the idea exact. There are three ways to handle a conflict, and one kind of rule that none of them can save.

The cheapest is to avoid it. Give every record a home region and send all its writes there. M-0042 is homed in eu, so a reader in Virginia that writes M-0042's holds goes to the eu leader and pays the round trip. Most traffic is local, and stays fast. The rule breaks when the home moves: eu fails and us takes M-0042's writes, or the shop moves its business. For that window, two leaders write the same rows.

Ids need the same care. Two leaders that each hand out the next number from one counter will issue the same number twice. That's why pgactive's README, the file that introduces it, lists "the lack of certain convenient database features such as incremental integer sequences" among the things an app must handle. Give each region its own range of numbers, or use UUIDs, random ids so long that two never match.

The second way is to let the last write win. Every change carries a timestamp, and every leader keeps the higher one. The leaders end up agreeing, and one of two concurrent writes disappears with no error. DynamoDB, Amazon's cloud database, does this for each item (its word for a row) in the default mode of its global tables, tables copied across regions. pgactive does it when two leaders insert or update the same row, keeping the row with the newest timestamp. How much it loses depends on how often two regions write the same row within the copying delay.

In this lesson's lab, two regions add holds to one shop, with 20 to 80 ms of delay. With writes 5 s apart in each region, 1% of confirmed holds vanish; 300 ms apart, 12.5%; 50 ms apart, 38.5%. Last write wins is safe only when each key is written once, such as inserts with unique ids.

The third way is to keep both and merge. Each change records which writes its leader had seen. A leader that gets a change it can't order against its own keeps both versions, called siblings, and the next reader merges them. Holds are only ever added, so taking every hold from both versions is a correct merge here, and the lab's detector loses nothing at any rate. Deletes are harder, because combining two versions brings removed items back. Lesson 8 fixes that with CRDTs, data types built to merge. The merge can also be your own code that runs on each conflict. pgactive's documentation describes a custom conflict handler next to last update wins, though the same documentation calls that feature planned, so check the version you run.

Some rules no merge can repair. Two regions each approve a 600 payment against a balance of 1,000, and each was right about its own copy. Keeping both writes breaks the rule. Dropping one throws away a payment the customer was told was approved. A rule like that needs the regions to agree before the write commits, which is what some of the next section's products do.

try.title: How loss depends on how often two regions write
steps: ContentionDemo.kt runs the lab's setup: two regions, 300 holds added in each, 20 to 80 ms of delay between them. It runs once with last write wins and once with the conflict detector, for six write rates.
Predict the share lost under last write wins when each region writes every 300 ms on average. Then run it.
Run it with another seed, the number that starts its random choices, with -Pargs='7', and check which numbers move.

code.title: from the labs folder
code.html: ./gradlew :sim:demo -Pmain=sfz.repl.l05.demo.ContentionDemoKt -q ./gradlew :sim:demo -Pmain=sfz.repl.l05.demo.ContentionDemoKt -Pargs='7' -q

try.expect:
600 acknowledged writes (300 per region), lag 20 to 80 ms, seed 42
mean gap between writes   last write wins lost   detector lost
     5,000 ms per region       6  ( 1.0%)             0
     1,000 ms per region      23  ( 3.8%)             0
       300 ms per region      75  (12.5%)             0
       100 ms per region     158  (26.3%)             0
        50 ms per region     231  (38.5%)             0
        10 ms per region     330  (55.0%)             0

The loss rate follows contention: the more often both regions write the same row inside one delay window, the more writes last write wins throws away. It never reaches zero, because even at one write every 5 seconds, two writes sometimes land within 80 ms of each other. With seed 7 the rows read 0.7%, 4.2%, 12.2%, 26.3%, 37.8% and 51.0%, so the rates come from the workload, not from luck. The detector column stays at 0 for every seed. Every run takes well under a second, because the simulation moves its own clock forward instead of waiting.

sections.h: Multi-region products: who takes writes for a row, and does a write wait
sections.html:
Many products sold as multi-region, meaning they run in several regions at once, aren't multi-leader in this lesson's sense. Ask two questions of each one. How many places accept a write for the same row? And does a write wait for another region before it commits?

waits for another region doesn't wait
one writer per row CockroachDB (Raft per range) Aurora Global Database
several writers per row DynamoDB global tables, MRSC; MySQL Group Replication, multi-primary DynamoDB global tables, MREC; pgactive

Aurora Global Database, Amazon's cloud database built on MySQL or PostgreSQL, has one primary region that takes writes, and read-only copies in other regions, fed asynchronously. A planned switch waits for the chosen copy to catch up, so it loses nothing. An unplanned failover can lose whatever hadn't crossed yet. That loss is the RPO (recovery point objective: how much recent data you may lose), and AWS, Amazon's cloud business, says it's "typically measured in seconds". Write forwarding lets a program in another region send writes, but they still go to the one writer.

CockroachDB is a database that spreads each table over many machines. It copies each range of rows with Raft, a way for a group of machines to agree on one order (the Consistency and consensus track builds it). So one copy, the leaseholder, orders each range's writes. A table declared REGIONAL BY ROW keeps each row's home region in a hidden crdb_region column, so rows homed in your region get fast reads and writes that are always up to date. That's this lesson's home region, built into the database. Surviving the loss of a whole region needs at least three regions and raises the number of copies from 3 to 5. It also adds at least one round trip to the nearest region to every write.

DynamoDB global tables choose a mode when the table is created, for good. MREC (multi-Region eventual consistency, the default) is true multi-leader. It copies changes "typically within a second or less", and for each item the last writer wins. The documentation spells out what follows. A strongly consistent read, the kind meant to return the latest version, can return old data if the item was last written in another Region. A conditional write, one that succeeds only if a check passes, checks only its own Region's copy. And a transaction is all-or-nothing only in the Region that ran it.

MRSC (multi-Region strong consistency) copies each write to at least one other Region before it returns, so a strongly consistent read anywhere sees the latest version. It asks a lot in return. It needs exactly three Regions: three copies, or two and a witness that holds data but answers no requests. The table must start empty, and no copies can be added later. It also gives up TTL (automatic expiry of items), local secondary indexes (one kind of extra lookup table) and transactions. A write to an item that another Region is changing fails with ReplicatedWriteConflictException, and you retry.

MySQL Group Replication, a feature of the free database MySQL, lets up to 9 servers take writes in its multi-primary mode. It checks each transaction against concurrent ones from the other servers. When two touch the same row, the one placed first in the group's order commits everywhere, and the other is undone. The manual calls this "a distributed first commit wins rule". Every commit waits for the group to agree on an order, and some database features don't work in this mode (the deeper section lists them).

For money, give each row one writer at a time, by home region or by agreement. Keep last write wins for data where losing one of two concurrent writes costs nothing, such as a shop's display name.

Every leader in this lesson was a server in a data center. Next, we'll put a leader on each laptop and phone.

try.title: One retried payment under MREC and MRSC rules
steps: Read the comment at the top of IdempotencyDemo.kt. It's a toy model of the two modes as the DynamoDB documentation describes them, not DynamoDB itself. (The file's name comes from idempotency: a retry with the same key has the same effect as one try.)
Predict how many times the card is charged under each mode, then run it.
try.expect:
-- MREC (eventual): the condition is checked against the local Region's copy --
t=0    eu condition passes, card charged (charge #1)
t=200  us condition passes, card charged (charge #2)
t=900  both copies converge on one item: us-result
charges: 2 for one checkout

-- MRSC (strong): writes replicate synchronously; a racing write fails --
t=0    eu condition passes, card charged (charge #1), write returns at t=250
t=200  us ReplicatedWriteConflictException: item is being modified in another Region
t=300  us ConditionalCheckFailed: replay the stored result
charges: 1 for one checkout

Under MREC, attribute_not_exists ("no item with this key yet") was true in both Regions, because us hadn't received eu's item yet. Both charged, and last writer wins later keeps one item, which hides the evidence. Under MRSC, the retry ran into the first write while it was still being copied, got ReplicatedWriteConflictException, retried 100 ms later, found the key and replayed the stored result. The price shows too: the eu write took 250 ms to return, because it waited for another Region.

refs.title: Amazon DynamoDB: how global tables work (MREC and MRSC)
MySQL 8.4: Group Replication background (certification, first commit wins)
Aurora Global Database: switchover and failover

opening:
Picture a payments company with customers in Europe and America. Its database takes every write in Virginia. A card tap in Frankfurt crosses the ocean and back before the reader beeps, and a payment that needs four steps makes that trip four times.

So the company runs a second database in Frankfurt and lets it take writes too. Taps are fast again. Then one evening a tap in Frankfurt times out, and the card reader tries again through Virginia. Each database checks whether it has seen this payment before. Each says no, and the customer pays twice.

It's easy to think that two databases copying each other behave like one database in two places. They do copy each other, but a fraction of a second late, and each checks its rules against its own copy.

In PostgreSQL replication, backups and failover, one primary took every write. In this lesson, we'll give each region a leader, watch two confirmed writes become one, and weigh the ways to handle a conflict. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a customer who paid twice: two databases, each sure it had never seen the payment. Each region was right about its own copy, a fraction of a second behind the other. So we give money one writer at a time, and save last write wins for data where losing a write costs nothing.

If you use a notes or calendar app on two devices, change the same entry on both while one is offline, then reconnect. See whether one change vanishes, or the app shows you both.

Next, we'll put a leader on every laptop and phone, and find out how an app merges changes made hours apart.

compare.title: Two Regions, one retried payment: the two DynamoDB global table modes

a.label: MREC (eventual, the default)
a.title: MREC (eventual, the default)
a.html:
eu  t=0    put idem-7f3a if attribute_not_exists   -> OK (checks eu's copy)
us  t=200  put idem-7f3a if attribute_not_exists   -> OK (us hasn't seen eu's item)
           two charges
later      replication: last writer wins per item  -> one item survives

write latency: local
RPO: the replication delay, usually a few seconds

b.label: MRSC (strong, exactly 3 Regions)
b.title: MRSC (strong, exactly 3 Regions)
b.html:
eu  t=0    put idem-7f3a if attribute_not_exists   -> OK after another Region has it
us  t=200  put idem-7f3a                           -> ReplicatedWriteConflictException
us  t=300  retry                                   -> ConditionalCheckFailed: replay
           one charge

write latency: at least one cross-Region round trip
RPO: 0; no TTL, no LSIs, no transactions

compare.note: Both modes accept writes in every Region; the difference is when the Regions find out about each other. MREC finds out after both writes have committed, so it can only pick a winner, and a condition is only as good as the local copy it checked. MRSC finds out before the write returns, so it can refuse one of the two and let the caller retry against the latest version. That costs a round trip to another Region on every write, and rules out features that need quick local work done later, such as automatic expiry.

worked.title: Putting a payments app in two regions without double charges

steps.say: List each table, where its writes come from, and what losing one of two concurrent writes would mean. Be concrete.
steps.code:
table              written from         lose one of two concurrent writes?
idempotency_keys   any region           a double charge
balances           any region           money moves twice or not at all
merchant_profile   back office, rare    a stale display name for a while
holds              terminals, constant  an authorization hold forgotten

steps.say: Home every shop in one region and send its money writes there. A request in the other region pays one round trip, for that shop only.
steps.code: fun writerFor(merchant: Merchant): DataSource = if (merchant.homeRegion == localRegion) localLeader // about 1 ms else leaders.getValue(merchant.homeRegion) // about 70 ms, but one writer per row

steps.say: Stop leaders handing out the same ids. PostgreSQL 18 makes UUIDs that start with the time (uuidv7()), so ids from both regions never collide and still sort roughly by time.
steps.code: CREATE TABLE holds ( id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(), merchant_id text NOT NULL, amount_minor bigint NOT NULL );

steps.say: Write down what happens when a home region is down. Either refuse money writes for its shops until it returns (one writer, some downtime), or move their home and accept that rows written in both places during the switch will conflict. Decide per table, before the outage.
steps.code:
eu down, merchant homed in eu:
  idempotency_keys, balances -> refuse: 503 for those merchants
  merchant_profile           -> accept in us; last write wins when eu returns
  holds                      -> accept in us; insert-only with uuidv7 ids, nothing to conflict

steps.say: Measure conflicts instead of guessing. With pgactive, set pgactive.log_conflicts_to_table to true and count what lands in its history table. Any conflict on a money table means a write went to the wrong region.
steps.code: SELECT count(*) FROM pgactive.pgactive_conflict_history;

lab.title: Two regions, last write wins, and a conflict detector
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. No Docker needed. All 11 fail with NotImplementedError.

Read Regions.kt, which is given. Each region is a leader for shop M-0042's holds. simulate runs writes and copying on its own clock, with a random delay per message, so messages overtake each other and a minute of traffic runs in milliseconds. Every write records in seen the ids of all the writes its region knew about.

In Conflicts.kt, write lastWriteWins. Its test and the two last-write-wins simulations pass. Read the steady-traffic test: 600 confirmed writes, more than 150 of them lost, and the regions still agree.
Write order from the seen sets alone. Never look at the timestamps.

Write applyDetecting. The rest pass, including the clock-skew test (one region's clock off) and a jqwik property, a test that tries many random seeds with two to four regions and checks that nothing is ever lost.
Experiment: make order use timestamps instead (a.timestamp < b.timestamp means BEFORE). See which tests fail, and why. Then put it back.
hints: compareValuesBy(a, b, Write::timestamp, Write::region) compares by timestamp, then by region name.
order is a when with four branches: SAME first, then a.id in b.seen, then b.id in a.seen, then CONCURRENT.
In applyDetecting, an incoming write that is SAME as or BEFORE any current version changes nothing.
Otherwise keep current.filter { order(it, incoming) == Order.CONCURRENT }, add incoming, and report a conflict when that filtered list isn't empty.
Region.read() returns every hold from all the siblings together. That union is the app's merge.

drill.title: Three regions and four rules, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking: (a) sketch three leaders in all-to-all, and the timeline in which an UPDATE reaches the third region before its INSERT; (b) say what discarding, last write wins and holding the update each do with it; (c) name the four ways to handle a conflict and what each one costs; (d) fill the two-by-two grid of one or several writers per row against waits or doesn't wait for another region, with one product in each cell.

answer.html:
(a) eu --INSERT--> us (fast)  eu --INSERT--> ap (slow)
    us applies INSERT, then UPDATE --> ap (fast): ap sees UPDATE first
(b) discard: ap keeps the INSERT's row, regions disagree forever
    last write wins: agree, but a slow clock can make the UPDATE lose everywhere
    hold until what the UPDATE's origin had seen is applied: right answer, any clocks
(c) avoid (home region): breaks when the home moves; ids need ranges or UUIDs
    last write wins: converges, silently drops one of two concurrent writes
    keep siblings and merge: no loss, but someone must merge; deletes need CRDTs
    agree before commit: no conflicts, a cross-region round trip per write
(d)                      waits                       doesn't wait
    one writer per row   CockroachDB                 Aurora Global Database
    several writers      DynamoDB MRSC, MySQL GR     DynamoDB MREC, pgactive

recap: Multi-leader replication puts a leader in each region (or on each device). Writes commit locally in about a millisecond and are copied to the other leaders asynchronously, so a region or a link can fail without stopping writes.

The cost is conflicts: two leaders accept writes to the same row before either has seen the other's. Rules that must see every write, such as a unique payment key or a balance at zero or above, can only be checked against a local copy.

Circles and stars depend on single nodes; all-to-all doesn't, but changes overtake each other, so an UPDATE can reach a region before its INSERT. Origin names stop loops. Timestamps can't order the changes, and recording what each change had seen can.

Handle a conflict by avoiding it (a home region per record), by last write wins (it agrees and silently loses: 1% to 55% of confirmed writes in the lab, depending on how often both regions write), or by keeping siblings and merging.

Products: Aurora Global has one asynchronous writer; CockroachDB orders each range with Raft and homes rows with REGIONAL BY ROW; DynamoDB MREC lets the last writer win, with checks against the local copy; MRSC waits for another Region and rejects racing writes; MySQL Group Replication lets the first-ordered transaction win.

The limit: no design gives fast local writes and one agreed answer at once. A rule like a balance that must stay positive needs the regions to agree before the write commits, and that wait is the round trip multi-leader was meant to avoid.

explain.prompt: A colleague asks why the team can't switch the payments table in DynamoDB to take writes in both regions, since the app would get faster. Explain what happens to two concurrent writes and to a conditional write, and what you'd do instead.
explain.answer: In the default mode, MREC, each region saves writes locally and copies them to the other within about a second. If both regions change the same item inside that second, neither knew about the other, and when the copies meet, DynamoDB keeps the one with the later internal timestamp and drops the other without an error. Conditional writes don't protect us either, because each region checks the condition against its own copy. A retried payment with the same payment key passes the "not seen yet" check in both regions and charges the card twice, and a transaction is only all-or-nothing in the region that ran it. For tables that move money, I'd give every shop a home region and send its money writes there. Or I'd use MRSC, which waits for another region before returning and fails a racing write with ReplicatedWriteConflictException, so we can retry. MRSC costs a round trip to another region on every write and needs exactly three regions, with no transactions or automatic expiry. Data where losing one of two concurrent writes is harmless, like a shop's display name, can use MREC and keep the speed.

deeper.html:
When one leader briefly became two. GitHub's October 2018 outage shows what happens when a single-leader system acts like a multi-leader one for a few minutes. A 43-second network cut between data centers on the US East Coast led its failover tooling to promote primaries in US West. Programs wrote there for about 40 minutes, while the East primaries still held several seconds of writes that had never been copied. Each side now had writes the other lacked, so switching back wasn't safe, and the East Coast programs couldn't live with a cross-country round trip on most queries. The service was degraded for 24 hours and 11 minutes. The write-up is worth reading in full for how the team decided which writes to keep: https://github.blog/news-insights/company-news/oct21-post-incident-analysis/

pgactive's family. pgactive descends from BDR (Bi-Directional Replication), a PostgreSQL extension built on reading row changes out of the WAL, and the same ideas live on in paid PostgreSQL distributions. Its conflict documentation is a useful catalogue even if you never run it. It lists INSERT/INSERT, UPDATE/UPDATE, UPDATE/DELETE and INSERT/UPDATE conflicts (the overtaking case), and conflicts on foreign keys and exclusion constraints. It explains why it refuses exclusion constraints altogether: on servers that work apart, no one can promise that no two rows overlap.

MySQL Group Replication's limits in multi-primary mode. The SERIALIZABLE isolation level is refused. Cascading foreign keys (a delete in one table that deletes rows in another) can produce conflicts it doesn't notice. Changing a table's shape on one server while another writes to it isn't supported. And SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks aren't shared across servers, so a lock taken on one server doesn't stop a write on another.

Further reading. The second edition of Designing Data-Intensive Applications (Kleppmann and Riccomini), chapter 6, covers multi-leader topologies, avoiding conflicts, agreeing on a value, and the sync engines of the next lesson in more depth, and points to the papers behind them. Lesson 8 of this track picks up the thread with version vectors and CRDTs, the tools that make "keep both and merge" practical.
